{"sample_id": "blind-70c5f350fedc45a382e4d096b70a5317", "theorem": "Consider a prime $p$ of the form $4 t+3$. Show that $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$ iff $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "number_theory", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), so \(m\) is odd.

Suppose first that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\). Then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Thus \(a^m\not\equiv1\pmod p\), while \((a^m)^2\equiv1\pmod p\). Since \(p\) is odd, \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Therefore
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
If \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \(a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\). Hence \(2m\mid2n\), so \(m\mid n\). Since \((-a)^m\equiv1\pmod p\), it follows that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\), and put \(x=-a\). Then \(x\) has odd order \(m\), and
\[
a^{2m}=(-x)^{2m}=x^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Suppose \(a^n=(-x)^n\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(n\) were odd, then \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod p\). Squaring gives \(x^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid2n\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(m\mid n\), which would give \(x^n\equiv1\pmod p\), contradicting \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod p\) because \(p\) is odd. Thus \(n\) is even. Consequently \(x^n=(-x)^n=a^n\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid n\). Since \(m\) is odd and \(n\) is even, \(2m\mid n\). Therefore every positive exponent annihilating \(a\) is divisible by \(2m\), while \(a^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p\). Hence \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=2m=p-1\), so \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\)."}
